stance_basis: issues formal Section 4(f) determination finding no feasible alternatives and approving the project
summary: The Deputy Administrator issued a formal Section 4(f) determination finding that there are no feasible and prudent alternatives to the temporary use of land from Woodrow Wilson Woods and that all possible planning to minimize harm has been included. The determination approves the reconstruction of U.S. Route 30 (Lincoln Highway) between Cicero Avenue and Chicago Road, noting that only a temporary construction easement of 0.17 acre is required and that all disturbed areas will be restored to their original state.
complaint_summary: The Deputy Administrator issues a formal Section 4(f) determination approving the reconstruction of U.S. Route 30, finding no feasible and prudent alternatives to the temporary use of 0.17 acre from Woodrow Wilson Woods and that all possible planning to minimize harm has been undertaken.

statement.text:
it is our finding that (1) there are no feasible and prudent alternatives to the use of land from Woodrow Wilson Woods of the Thorn Creek Division of the Cook County Forest Preserve District along Lincoln Highway (U.S. Route 30), and (2) the highway proposal includes all possible planning to minimize harm resulting from such use.
The project involves reconstruction of the present highway and bridge for Lincoln Highway from Cicero Avenue to Chicago Road. The present highway is an undivided 40 foot, urban-type facility with curb and gutter and a closed drainage system. Lincoln Highway is a major east-west highway. Present automobile and truck volumes exceed the capacity of the highway causing congestion and above-normal accident rates. This section of highway is structurally and functionally obsolete because of deteriorating pavement and structures, drainage problems, traffic congestion, and accident experience.
The proposed reconstruction will provide a divided (14-foot to 16-foot median) modern highway. The proposed highway will have six lanes between Cicero Avenue and Western Avenue and four lanes between Western Avenue and Chicago Road. It will be an urban-type facility with curb and gutter and a closed drainage system.
The Woodrow Wilson Woods is approximately 31 acres and is owned by the Cook County Forest Preserve District. This Forest Preserve includes open areas for picnicking and wooded areas for hiking with a parking lot area and a foot bridge. Lincoln Highway forms the southern boundary of Woodrow Wilson Woods and provides vehicle access.
The proposed improvement will require a temporary construction easement of 0.17 acre from Woodrow Wilson Woods for the removal and reconstruction of the bridge over Thorn Creek and to rebuild the driveway that provides access to the Woodrow Wilson Woods parking area.

No existing or proposed facilities in the Woodrow Wilson Woods will be affected by the implementation of the proposal. However, during construction, there will be minor inconveniences for the vehicular traffic into and out of the area. Access will be maintained to the parking facility throughout the reconstruction of the roadway, and there will be no effect on pedestrian access.
The capacity and structural integrity of the present highway are inadequate for today's transportation needs. The modernization of Lincoln Highway is recognized as a high-priority item in the transportation improvement plan for the region because of the highway's inadequacies, high maintenance costs, and high accident rate. Reconstruction of the bridge without widening would provide a structurally adequate facility; however, such an alternate is not considered feasible and prudent because it would continue the present congested conditions, excessive accidents, and inadequate hydraulic requirements. Even this alternative would require encroachment on the Forest Preserve to remove the existing bridge.
No land will be taken on a permanent basis from the Cook County Forest Preserve. The construction of a new curb, gutter, and shoulders on the existing right-of-way will improve the esthetics of the roadside. In addition to the standard erosion and soil conservation control precautions for Illinois highway construction, timely plantings will be placed for erosion control. All areas involved in the temporary construction easement that are disturbed by construction work or changes in grade will be regraded, topsoiled, fertilized, and sodded in order to return the land to its original state.
